speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Well, in terms of changes, we ask our hospitals, including our rural hospitals, to do the hardest thing you could possibly ask them to do, which is stop all the income. You can possibly stop all of the elective surgery. Anything you think you don't have to do, don't do it. And by the way, don't get paid for it because you haven't done it. But stand ready to deal with the worst health care issue, problem your communities ever had to deal with. So keep your spending at a high level, keep your income at a low level and see what happens. And the answer, of course, to what happens is it doesn't produce a very good result. So one of the things we did first was provide some provider relief to hospitals and doctors and other providers. We talk about provider relief, about 80% of health, federal health care money. Goes to hospitals in about 20% goes to clinics and doctors and other things but to provide that provider relief as much as possible to make it relief that Wouldn't have to be paid back by rural hospitals particularly and to look at ways they could provide services in a different way and so telehealth and became a much bigger part of the healthcare picture in 2020. I've been arguing for about five years of whether it was behavioral health or any other kind of health. The telehealth was critically important to people in outstate Missouri, people in rural areas, people that are hour or two or more away from their doctor and maybe even more than that away from their specialist if they have to go to a special doctor. And we've really made big steps forward there. A lot of that has now been made permanent and all of it that wasn't made permanent has been extended through at least the end of this year. Some of it into early next year by the federal agency that manages who pays the Medicare dollar, who pays the Medicaid dollar. But most of this is really driven by whether Medicare will pay or not. And it is paying now. And I've talked to lots of doctors on this topic, Spencer. And when you say just, I try not to prejudice the question that I say, how many times out of 100 is that telehealth visit as good as a visit where somebody makes the effort to come and be in the same room with you? And the answer is always, well, way more than nine out of 10 times, way more than 90 times out of 100. And then if you've got a nurse practitioner or a clinic or somebody you probably even narrow that down to where the specialist doesn't need to actually be in the room with you, but doesn't need to be able to see you and talk to you and ask questions that you can answer yourself or with just a little bit of help are able to answer. So rural clinics suddenly become an open door that opens. to health care in ways that they haven't been able to be before. And most importantly, if the government pays for it, and usually if the government will pay for it, your insurance company will also pay for it. A lot of insurance companies follow sort of the Medicare rule of, well, should this be an insured item or not? And telehealth and telebehavioral health, you know, lots of people who had an opioid challenge or another behavioral health challenge, have had real challenges during what we've gone through this year. One, the increased isolation that a lot of people had to the concern that you or somebody in your family had lost your job or might lose your job or that somebody in your family had a health challenge that too many times resulted in actually losing that person. all of those things made the behavioral health challenge greater. So it's also something that you can deliver pretty effectively through a telehealth situation. I think that's probably the biggest step forward with rural health. But also, I think we drew a lot of attention finally to what I've been saying and others have been saying, frankly, since the passage of the Affordable Care Act in that rural hospitals and rural health providers are not adequately dealt with in what is happening and likely to happen under this greater government belief that everybody will just have insurance. And so it'll all work out. You don't have to have the kind of special help for hospitals that really are there and is the only place that people can go. And if that hospital goes away, that healthcare beachhead goes away as well.
